mice.e: From Middle English mys, mice, muis, mise, mis, from Old English mȳs (“mice”), from an umlauted form of Proto-Germanic *mūsiz (“mice”), nominative and vocative plural of Proto-Germanic *mūs (“mouse”).
mice.g: To be distracted or inattentive (possibly alluding to a cat being distracted by a mouse).

midair.g: In the act of flight; airborne.

midday.e: From Middle English midday, from Old English middæġ (“midday, noon”), equivalent to mid- + day.
midday.g: Noon; twelve o'clock during the day.

middle.e: From Middle English myddel, middel, from Old English middel (“middle, centre, waist”), from Proto-Germanic *midlą, *midilą, *medalą (“middle”), a diminutive of Proto-Germanic *midjō (“middle, midst”) (compare *midjaz (“mid, middle”, adjective)), from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between, in the middle, middle”).

midnight.e: From Middle English midnight, from Old English midniht, from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts (“midnight”), equivalent to mid- + night.
midnight.g: The middle of the night: the sixth temporal hour, equidistant between sunset and sunrise.

midst.e: From Middle English middes, midst, myddest (“middle”), from Old English midde, reshaped in Middle English phrases like in middes (“in the middle”) by analogy with adverbs in -(e)s; also compare Old English on middan, tōmiddes. Forms in -(e)st are probably due to influence of superlatives.
midst.g: A place in the middle of something; may be used of a literal or metaphorical location.

midwife.e: From Middle English midwif, corresponding to mid (“with”) + wif (“woman, wife, female”). It appears not to be entirely clear whether the original understanding was “with-woman” in the sense of “attending/assisting woman”, or “they who are with the woman” (namely the mother).
midwife.g: A person, usually a woman, who is trained to assist women in childbirth, but who is not a physician.

might.e: From Old English meahte and mihte, inflections of magan, whence English may.

mightily.e: From Middle English mightili (“with might, powerfully, strongly; forcefully, violently; greatly; etc.”), from Old English meahtiglice (“with might, powerfully, mightily”), from meahtiġ, mihtiġ (“powerful, mighty”) + -līċe (suffix forming adverbs). Mihtiġ is derived from Proto-Germanic *mahtīgaz (“mighty”), from *mahtiz (“force, strength.

mighty.e: From Middle English mighty, mightie, mighti, myghty, miȝty, maȝty, from Old English mihtiġ, mehtiġ, meahtiġ, mæhtiġ (“mighty”), from Proto-West Germanic *mahtīg (“mighty”), from Proto-Germanic *mahtīgaz (“mighty”), equivalent to might + -y.
mighty.g: A warrior of great strength and courage.

migration.e: From Middle French migration and its source, Latin migrātiō, from the participle stem of migrō (“to migrate”). Morphologically migrate + -ion.
migration.g: An instance of moving to live in another place for a while.

milch.e: From Middle English mylche, melche, from Old English *melċe, *milċe (attested in þrimilċe, þrimilċemōnaþ), from Proto-West Germanic *milkī, *malkī, from Proto-Germanic *melkaz (“milky, milk-giving”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ- (“to wipe, wipe off, milk”).

mildew.e: From Middle English myldew, from Old English mildēaw, meledēaw, from Proto-West Germanic *milidauw, from *mili (“honey”) + *dauw (“dew”).
mildew.g: A growth of minute powdery or webby fungi, whitish or of different colors, found on various diseased or decaying substances.

mildness.e: From Middle English mildenesse, from Old English mildnes, mildness, equivalent to mild + -ness.
mildness.g: The quality of being mild; gentleness.

mile.e: From Middle English myle, mile, from Old English mīl, from Proto-West Germanic *mīliju, a borrowing of Latin mīlia, mīllia, plural of mīle, mīlle (“mile”) (literally ‘thousand’ but used as a short form of mīlle passūs (“a thousand paces”)).
mile.g: The international mile: a unit of length precisely equal to 1.609344 kilometers established by treaty among Anglophone nations in 1959, divi

military.e: From Middle English militari, from Old French militaire, from Latin mīlitāris, from mīles (“soldier”) + -āris (whence -ary).
military.g: Characteristic of members of the armed forces.

milk.e: From Middle English mylk, milk, from Old English meolc, meoluc (“milk”), from Proto-West Germanic *meluk (“milk”), from Proto-Germanic *meluks (“milk”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ- (“milk, to milk”).
milk.g: A white liquid produced by the mammary glands of female mammals to nourish their young. From certain animals, especially cows, it is also ca

milk.e: From Middle English mylken, from Old English melcan, from Proto-Germanic *melkaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-, the same root as the noun.
milk.g: To express milk from (a mammal, especially a cow).

mill.e: From Middle English mylne, mille, from Old English mylen, from Proto-West Germanic *mulīnu (“mill”), from Late Latin molīna, molīnum, molīnus (“mill”), from Latin molō (“grind, mill”, verb), closely allied to Proto-Germanic *muljaną (“to crush, grind”) (see English millstone). Perhaps cognate with Milne (a surname).
mill.g: A grinding apparatus for substances such as grains, seeds, etc. (Some are small and simple, and some are large and complex.)

mill.e: Ultimately from Latin mīllēsimum. The clipping comes by way of the clipped word, millimetre.

millet.e: From late Middle English, borrowed from Middle French millet; from Latin milium, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”), see also Ancient Greek μελίνη (melínē, “millet”) and Lithuanian málnos (“millet”). Not related to مِلَّة (milla).
millet.g: Any of a group of various types of grass or its grains used as food, widely cultivated in the developing world.

millet.e: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish ملت (millet), from Arabic مِلَّة (milla).
millet.g: A semi-autonomous confessional community under the Ottoman Empire, especially a non-Muslim one.

million.e: From Middle English milioun, from Middle French milion, from Old French millon, from Italian milione (“million”, from mille (“thousand”, from Latin mille) + -one).
million.g: The cardinal number 1 000 000: 10⁶; a thousand thousand (1,000²).

millstone.e: From Middle English mylneston, milneston, from Old English mylenstān (“millstone”), from Proto-West Germanic *mulīnu + *stain; equivalent to mill + stone.
millstone.g: A large round stone used for grinding grain.

mina.e: Borrowed from Hindi मैना (mainā)/Urdu مینا (mainā), from Sanskrit मदन (madana).
Borrowed from Latin mina, from Ancient Greek μνᾶ (mnâ, “mna”).
mina.g: A monetary unit of ancient Greece and the Middle East, originally equivalent to the weight of a mina of silver.

mince.e: From Middle English mincen, minsen; partly from Old English minsian, ġeminsian (“to make less, make smaller, diminish”), from Proto-West Germanic *minnisōn, from Proto-Germanic *minnisōną (“to make less”); partly from Old French mincer, mincier (“to cut into small pieces”), from mince (“slender, slight, puny”).

mind.e: From Middle English minde, munde, imynde, imunde, ȝemynde, ȝemunde, from Old English mynd, ġemynd (“mind, memory”), from Proto-West Germanic *mundi, *gamundi, from Proto-Germanic *mundiz, *gamundiz (“memory, remembrance”), from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”) (compare also mantis, via Greek), from the root *men- (“to think”).

mindful.e: From Middle English myndeful, myndefull, from Old English ġemyndful (“of good memory”), equivalent to mind + -ful.

mindful.g: As much as can be held in one's mind at a time.

minding.e: From Middle English mynding, myndyng, equivalent to mind + -ing.
minding.g: The act of taking heed of something.

mine.e: From Middle English min, myn, from Old English mīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mīn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *méynos.
mine.g: That or those belonging to me.

mine.e: From Middle English, from Old French mine, from Late Latin mina, from Gaulish (compare to Welsh mwyn, Irish mianach (“ore”)), from Proto-Celtic *meinis (“ore, metal”).
mine.g: An excavation from which ore or solid minerals are taken, especially one consisting of underground tunnels.

miner.e: From mine + -er (agent noun suffix) or + -er (occupational suffix).
miner.g: A person who works in a mine.

mingle.e: From earlier mingil, mengle, from Middle English menglen, equivalent to ming + -le.
mingle.g: To intermix; to combine or join, as an individual or part, with other parts, but commonly so as to be distinguishable in the product.

minish.e: From Middle English menuse, from Middle French menusier, from Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre.
minish.g: To lessen or cause to seem to be less.

minister.e: From Middle English ministre, from Old French ministre, from Latin minister (“an attendant, servant, assistant, a priest's assistant or other under official”), from minor (“less”) + -ter; see minor.
minister.g: A person who is trained to preach, to perform religious ceremonies, and to afford pastoral care at a Protestant church.

minister.e: From Middle English mynystren, from Middle French ministrer, from Old French menistrer, ministrer and Latin ministrō, from minister.
minister.g: To attend to (the needs of); to tend; to take care (of); to give aid; to give service.

ministration.e: From Middle English ministracioun, from Old French ministracïon, from Latin ministrātio; equivalent to minister + -ation.
ministration.g: The act of ministering; an instance of providing aid, care, or assistance.

ministry.e: From Middle English mynisterie, borrowed from Old French menistere, in turn borrowed itself from Latin ministerium; equivalent to minister + -y.
ministry.g: A government department at the administrative level, normally headed by a minister (or equivalent rank, e.g. secretary of state), who holds

minor.e: From Middle English minor, menor, menour, etc., from Latin minor (“lesser; young; young person”) both directly and via Norman and Middle French menor, menour, etc.
minor.g: Lesser, smaller in importance, size, degree, seriousness, or significance compared to another option, particularly

minstrel.e: Ministerium is derived from minister (“accomplice; agent; aide; attendant; servant; waiter”) (probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mey-n- (“little, small”) + *-yōs (“-er”, comparative suffix) + *-teros (contrastive or oppositional suffix forming adjectives)) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns).
minstrel.g: Originally, an entertainer employed to juggle, play music, sing, tell stories, etc.; a buffoon, a fool, a jester; later, a medieval (especia

mint.e: From Middle English mynt, münet (“money, coin”), from Old English mynet (“coin”), from late Proto-West Germanic *munit, from Latin monēta (“place for making coins, coined money”), from the temple of Juno Moneta (named for Monēta mother of the Muses), where coins were made. Old English mynetian (“to mint”) is a parallel formation.
mint.g: A building or institution where money (originally, only coins) is produced under government licence.

mint.e: From Middle English mynte, from Old English minte (“mint plant”), from Proto-West Germanic *mintā (“mint”), from Latin menta, probably from a lost Mediterranean language either through Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē), μίνθα (míntha) or directly.
mint.g: Any plant in the genus Mentha in the family Lamiaceae, typically aromatic with square stems.

minus.e: From Middle English mynus, from Latin minus, neuter form of minor, comparative form of parvus (“small, little”), from the Proto-Indo-European root *mey- (“few, small”).
minus.g: Made less or reduced by (followed by an expression of number or quantity).

miracle.e: From Middle English miracle, from Old French miracle, from Latin mīrāculum (“object of wonder”), from mīror (“to wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meyh₂- (“to smile, to be astonished”). Partially displaced native wonder, from Old English wundor (“miracle, wonder”).
miracle.g: An event that appears inexplicable by the laws of nature and so is held to be supernatural in origin.

miraculous.g: By supernatural or uncommon causes, e.g. by a god; that cannot be explained in terms of normal events.

mirage.e: An unadapted borrowing from French mirage c. 1812.
mirage.g: An optical phenomenon in which light is refracted through a layer of hot air close to the ground, often giving the illusion of a body of wat

mire.e: From Middle English mire, a borrowing from Old Norse mýrr, from Proto-Germanic *miuzijō, whence also Swedish myr, Norwegian myr, Icelandic mýri, Dutch *mier (in placenames, for example Mierlo).
From Middle English mire, myre, from Old English *mīere, from Proto-West Germanic *miurijā, from Proto-Germanic *miurijǭ (“ant”), from Proto-Indo-European *morwís (“ant”).

mirror.e: From Middle English mirour, from Old French mireor (“mirror”, literally “looker, watcher”), from mirer (“look at”), from Latin mīror (“wonder at”), from mīrus (“wonderful”), from Proto-Indo-European *smey- (“to laugh, to be glad”).
mirror.g: A smooth surface, usually made of glass with reflective material painted on the underside, that reflects light so as to give an image of wha

mirth.e: From Middle English merth, myrthe, murhthe, from Old English myrgþ (“mirth, joy”), from Proto-West Germanic *murgiþu (“briefness, brevity”); equivalent to merry + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
mirth.g: The emotion usually following humor and accompanied by laughter.

miry.e: From Middle English myry, equivalent to mire + -y.
miry.g: Resembling or characteristic of a mire; swampy, boggy.

miscarry.e: From Middle English miscarien. By surface analysis, mis- + carry.
miscarry.g: To have an unfortunate accident of some kind; to be killed, or come to harm.

mischief.e: From Middle English myschef, meschef, meschief, mischef, from Old French meschief, from meschever (“to bring to grief”), from mes- (“badly”) + chever (“happen; come to a head”), from Vulgar Latin *capare, from Latin caput (“head”).
mischief.g: Conduct that playfully causes petty annoyance.

mischief.e: From Middle English myschefen, myscheven, from Old French meschever.
mischief.g: To do a mischief to; to harm.

mischievous.e: From Middle English myschevous, mischevous, from Anglo-Norman meschevous, from Old French meschever, from mes- (“mis-”) + chever (“come to an end”) (from chef (“head”)). By surface analysis, mischief + -ous.

misdeed.e: From Middle English misdede, from Old English misdǣd (“misdeed”), from Proto-West Germanic *missadādi, from Proto-Germanic *missadēdiz (“misdeed”); equivalent to mis- + deed.
misdeed.g: That which was done that should not have been, ranging from any sin or moral offense to various degrees of crime.

miserable.e: Borrowed from Middle French miserable, from Old French, from Latin miserabilis, equivalent to miser + -able.
miserable.g: In a state of misery: very sad, ill, or poor.

miserably.e: From Middle English myserablie; equivalent to miserable + -ly.

misery.e: From Middle English miserie, from Old French miserie (modern: misère), from Latin miseria, from miser, equivalent to miser + -y.
misery.g: Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; distress; woe.

misguided.e: From misguide + -ed (suffix forming adjectives; and past tense and past participle forms of regular verbs).
misguided.g: Of a person: lacking proper guidance; misled or mistaken in one's actions or thinking.

misle.e: Probably a blend of mist + drizzle.
misle.g: A fine rain or thick mist; mizzle.

misle.e: From misled, the standard irregular past tense of mislead, being misconstrued as *misle + -ed.

mislead.e: From Middle English mysleden, from Old English mislǣdan (“to mislead”), from Proto-Germanic *missalaidijaną (“to mislead”). By surface analysis, mis- + lead.
mislead.g: To lead astray, in a false direction.

miss.e: Verb from Middle English missen, from Old English missan (“to miss, escape the notice of a person”), from Proto-West Germanic *missijan, from Proto-Germanic *missijaną (“to miss, go wrong, fail”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to change, exchange, trade”). Noun from Middle English misse, mis, from Old English miss (“loss, absence”).
miss.g: To fail to hit, catch, grasp, etc.
Alternative spelling of Miss when used as a term of address or title of respect.

missing.g: Not able to be located; gone, misplaced.

mission.e: Borrowed from Latin missiō, missiōnem (“a sending, sending away, dispatching, discharging, release, remission, cessation”).
mission.g: A set of tasks that fulfills a purpose or duty; an assignment set by an employer, or by oneself.

mistake.e: From Middle English mistaken, from Old Norse mistaka (“to take in error, to miscarry”); equivalent to mis- + take. The noun, which replaced earlier mistaking, is derived from the verb.
mistake.g: To understand wrongly, taking one thing or person for another.

mistress.e: From Middle English maistresse, from Old French maistresse (whence French maîtresse), feminine of maistre (“master”). By surface analysis, mist(e)r + -ess.
mistress.g: Of a woman: to master; to learn or develop to a high degree of proficiency.

misunderstand.e: From Middle English mys-understanden, equivalent to mis- + understand.
misunderstand.g: To understand incorrectly, while believing one has understood correctly.

misuse.g: An incorrect, improper or unlawful use of something.

mite.e: From Middle English mite, from Old English mīte (“mite, tiny insect”), from Proto-West Germanic *mītā, from Proto-Germanic *mītǭ (“biting insect”, literally “cutter”), from *maitaną (“to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“small”) or *meh₂y- (“to cut”).
mite.g: Any of many minute arachnids which, along with the ticks, comprise subclass Acari (syn. Acarina).

mitre.e: From Middle English mytre, from Old French mitre, from Ancient Greek μίτρα (mítra, “headband, turban”). Its use in reference to a counterfeit coin derived from the bishop's mitre stamped upon it.
mitre.g: A covering for the head, worn on solemn occasions by church dignitaries, which has been made in many reincarnations, most recently as a tall

mix.e: From Middle English mixen (attested in past tense as mixed, myxyd), from Old English *mixian, miscian, from Proto-West Germanic *miskijan, from Proto-West Germanic *miskijan (“to mix”), from Proto-Indo-European *miḱ-sḱé-ti, from *meyǵ-, *meyḱ- (“to mix”).
A merger of a nominal use of the verb and a borrowing from Anglo-Norman mixte, from Latin mixtus, past participle of misceō (“mix”). Nowadays regarded automatically as the nominal form of the verb.
mix.g: The result of mixing two or more substances; a mixture.

mixed.e: From mix, equivalent to mix + -ed. In adjectival use, reinforced by French mixte and/or Latin mixtus, past participle of misceō (“mix”), from the same Indo-European root as mix.
mixed.g: Having two or more separate aspects.

mixt.e: Alternative spelling of Early Modern mix'd, probably influenced by the synonymous Latin mixtus.
mixt.g: Archaic spelling of mixed, simple past and past participle of mix.

mixture.e: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French misture, from Latin mixtūra (“a mixing”), from mixtus, perfect passive participle of misceō (“mix”); compare mix.
